name: WP Umbrella
tagline: Monitoring, plugin updates, backups and white-label client reports for a fleet of WordPress sites.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: WordPress hands you most of this for free: the REST API plus an application password tells you core version, plugin versions, available updates and whether the site answers at all. A cron job, a SQLite table and an email sender covers uptime, an update inventory and a weekly digest in a weekend. Where it falls apart is the scary half: one-click bulk updates with a real rollback path, PHP fatal error capture, visual regression checks before and after an update, and off-server backups you have actually restored from. If you maintain three sites of your own, build it. If you bill clients for uptime and your reputation lives inside a PDF report, you are buying the parts you would cut corners on.
coreLoopDIY: A cron worker polls every WordPress site's REST API for uptime, core and plugin versions and pending updates, stores history in SQLite, and emails you a digest plus instant alerts when a site goes dark.
requirements: A small always-on host or VPS for the cron worker, not a laptop
An application password per WordPress site (admin level)
An SMTP or transactional email key for alerts
Optional SSH plus WP-CLI access on each host if you want real backups and updates
whatYouLose: Safe updates: staging clone, visual regression diff, automatic rollback when a plugin update blanks the page
PHP error and fatal monitoring, which needs a plugin dropped into every site, not a REST poll
Off-site incremental backups with a tested restore, plus somewhere to actually store them
White-label client reports that look like something you can invoice against
Multi-region uptime probes, so your single VPS having a bad network day becomes a false alarm storm
moatNotes: The integration surface is not the WordPress API, it is the long tail of hosts, cache layers and plugins that break in specific ways during an update.
whyPeopleStillPay: Agencies do not pay for the dashboard, they pay so that when a plugin update takes down a client's shop at 2am somebody other than them noticed and there is a backup that restores. That is a promise about the worst case, and a DIY cron job on one VPS makes a weaker version of that promise. Add the client-facing report that justifies a monthly retainer and the per-site price stops looking like the expensive option.
notes: Fine for your own sites, thin for a maintenance retainer. The part you cannot cheaply fake is the rollback path when an update goes wrong.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted WordPress fleet monitor. Single Node 22 + TypeScript project, no framework churn.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Fastify for the HTTP server, server-rendered HTML via plain template literals, no React
- better-sqlite3 for storage, single file data/fleet.db, schema created on boot
- node-cron for scheduling inside the same process
- nodemailer for alerts, SMTP creds from .env
- Everything in .env: SMTP_URL, ALERT_TO, DASHBOARD_TOKEN

Sites are configured in sites.json: name, baseUrl, wpUser, wpAppPassword. Never store credentials in the database file.

What it does:
1. Every 60 seconds, HEAD/GET each site homepage. Record status code and response time in a checks table. Two consecutive failures sends one alert email; recovery sends one more. No repeat spam.
2. Every 6 hours, call the WordPress REST API with basic auth from the application password: read core version, plugin list and versions, theme, PHP version if exposed. Store a snapshot row per site per run.
3. Diff the newest snapshot against the previous one and record update_available and version_changed events.
4. Weekly cron at Monday 08:00 sends a plain text digest per site: uptime percentage, slowest response, pending updates, plugins that changed.

Dashboard at / behind a single bearer token in the query string or a cookie: table of sites with current status, 30 day uptime bar, pending update count, and a per-site page listing snapshot history and recent incidents.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: performing updates, backups, staging clones, visual regression, PHP error capture, multi-user accounts, PDF reports, telemetry of any kind.

Deliver a README with .env.example, a sites.json.example, and a systemd unit file. Include a seed script that inserts fake check history so the dashboard is not empty on first run.
